opening.headline: Learn to isolate the causes of slow responses by breaking them down into the components of latency, and apply measures such as model rank, output length, and parallel calls in order of greatest effect.
body: Users complain that it takes too long to get an answer. The development team begins to guess whether the model is slow, the prompts are long, or the network is the problem. But if you guess, you'll be wasting time on things that don't work. The first step is to divide the delay into its components and determine which section is larger.

In this lesson, we will see that latency is divided into input processing, output generation, and network, and see how measures such as model rating, effort, output length, parallel calls, and streaming reduce each delay. Next, we explain the case of switching to a lightweight model from a quality verification perspective, and summarize the criteria for selecting the most effective means depending on the situation.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Describe the impact of model class, output length, and parallel calls on latency
Among the delay time reduction methods, you can choose one that is appropriate and effective for the situation.

screens.title: Slow response makes users uncomfortable
screens.lead: First, read the situation the development team faced. I read this while thinking about what to check first.

visual.alt: A scene where the loading sign takes a long time on the chat screen and the user leaves a complaint.
labels: It takes too long to get an answer

paragraphs: I was running a customer service app, and I received complaints from users. The point is that it takes too long to get an answer. The development team tries to guess the cause. Is the model slow, the prompts long, or the network the problem?

It's dangerous to start fixing things just by guessing. Difficulty reducing the prompts has little effect if most of the actual delay comes from output generation. If you change the model but the response is too long and slow, you have lost quality.

So the question in this class is how to divide the delay to see the cause. Only after dividing the cause into sections can we choose which measures, such as model class, output length, or parallel calls, will have the greatest effect.

callout.label: question of the day
callout.text: How can we divide the delay time to see the cause?

screens.outro: First, let's think about what we think is the biggest cause of delay.

screens.title: What is the biggest cause of delay?
screens.lead: What do you think is the biggest cause of latency? When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: When the input was long or the output was long, which did you feel took longer?
items.answer: Many people think that long prompts are the cause of the slowness, but it is usually the output that is long that causes the response to take too long. Output tokens are generated one by one in order, so the longer they are, the longer they take. The demonstration in this class specifically compares the magnitude of the effect input and output have on latency.

items.prompt: Aren't the requests being sent out multiple times in sequence?
items.answer: Since the round-trip time is accumulated for each request, a structure that sends sequentially in succession will add up to be slower. If you're sending requests out of order that don't depend on each other, the structure itself may be causing the delay.

items.prompt: What will users see while they wait?
items.answer: Even if it takes the same amount of time, waiting for a blank screen and watching the answer being written are two very different experiences. Reducing latency involves not only reducing actual processing time, but also making users feel like they're waiting less.

screens.outro: Now that we have the guesswork out of the way, let's break down the delay into its components.

screens.title: Breaking down latency into its components
screens.lead: Select a number marker to see a detailed description of each section that makes up the latency and ways to reduce it. Please select them in order starting from number 1.

visual.alt: A horizontal timeline where the latency from request transmission to response completion is divided into network, input processing, and output generation sections.

markers.label: network
markers.title: network round trip
markers.body: This is the communication time it takes to send a request and receive a response. Since each request costs one round trip time, the number of requests adds up and becomes large. You can reduce the number of round trips by combining multiple sequential steps into one prompt.

markers.label: Input processing
markers.title: Input processing
markers.body: This is the time the model reads the input token. The OpenAI documentation explains that reducing prompts by 50% can only improve latency by 1 to 5%. Unless the input is really large, like a document or image, reducing input is not a very effective measure. Instead, if you use a cache by gathering the parts that do not change in front, the input to be processed will be reduced.

markers.label: generate output
markers.title: generate output
markers.body: This is the time the model creates output tokens one by one in order. Token generation is almost always the step with the most latency, and the rule of thumb from the OpenAI documentation is that reducing the output tokens by 50% can reduce latency by close to 50%. Reducing output is the most direct means.

markers.label: first token
markers.title: Time to first token (TTFT)
markers.body: The time from when the request was sent until the model creates the first token. This is especially important for user responsiveness when streaming. If you can see the first letter quickly rather than having to wait for the entire response to complete, the perceived wait will be greatly reduced.

markers.label: measure
markers.title: Measure first
markers.body: You cannot know which section is large until you measure it. Measure the time for each section and choose the means starting from the largest section. The OpenAI document organizes latency optimization methods into seven principles: process faster, generate less, reduce inputs, reduce requests, parallelize, make users wait less, and don't rely on LLM.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified the components, let's start by looking at the model classes that have the biggest impact on speed.

screens.title: Model class and output length
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn how model size affects speed, model ratings by provider, and how to adjust effort and output length.

visual.alt: Illustration of a three-step ladder where the larger the model size, the higher the performance, but the speed and cost become disadvantageous.
labels: Small models are enhanced with prompts, examples, and fine tuning.

tabs.label: model size
tabs.body:
The factor that has the greatest impact on inference speed is the size of the model. Smaller models are usually faster and cheaper, and if used well, can even outperform larger models.

There are three ways to enhance the quality of small models: Write more detailed prompts, add few-shot examples, and fine-tune or distill. Reviewing this augmentation together before downgrading the model can reduce quality loss.

tabs.label: Rating by provider
tabs.body:
**Claude**: For apps where speed is critical, Claude Haiku 5.5 provides the fastest response while maintaining high intelligence. The documentation suggests that it is suitable for real-time applications, high-volume processing, and subagent tasks.

**OpenAI**: Luna is the most efficient and suitable for scoped tasks and frequent automation; Sol is suitable for complex tasks that require balance to manage time and cost; Astra is the highest performance and suitable for ambiguous problems and deep analysis. If cost and delay are not an issue, use Astra as the default, and if you want to reduce it, follow the instructions to choose a level.

tabs.label: effort
tabs.body:
Some of Claude's models use the effort parameter to trade intelligence, delay, and cost within a model. The documentation explains that adjusting effort is often a better measure than changing the model.

The cheapest and fastest level you can use is `output_config={"effort": "low"}` in Claude Haiku 5.5. At this time, considering the tokens to be used, leave some space in `max_tokens`. Before changing the model, the order is to adjust from effort to evaluation.

tabs.label: output length
tabs.body:
The output is the largest section of delay, so making it shorter is effective. If it's a natural language response, we ask you to be concise. For structured output, minimize the output syntax by shortening function names or omitting named arguments.

As a last resort, you can end the creation early with `max_tokens` or a stop token. The Claude document also advises to place a hard limit on the output length with `max_tokens`. The key is to gain more time by reducing one output token.

screens.outro: Now that we have the model class and output length confirmed, let's look at parallel calls and the rest of the means.

screens.title: Parallel calls and other means
screens.lead: Switch between the two states below to compare how the overall time changes when processing the same three-step tasks sequentially and in parallel.

visual.alt: Illustration comparing the timeline length when sending the same three requests sequentially and in parallel.

states.label: sequential processing
states.body:
If you send three requests one after another, the total time will be the sum of the times of all three requests. One round trip time is added for each request.

If requests that do not depend on each other are sent using this structure, the structure itself is the cause of the delay. You can reduce the number of requests by grouping steps that must be followed in order by numbering them into one prompt and receiving the results as named fields in JSON.

states.label: parallel processing
states.body:
Steps that are not strictly ordered to each other are sent simultaneously. Just as two sets of clothes take the same amount of time to dry as one, the total time is reduced by the slowest request.

Speculative execution is possible even in strictly sequential steps. For example, you start input inspection and body generation at the same time, and cancel creation if the inspection results are different from expectations. If the predictions are correct, inspection delays are virtually eliminated.

In addition, streaming is the most effective way to reduce waiting to less than 1 second, and if tasks that can be solved with rules are not left to the LLM but handled by hard coding, pre-calculation, or general UI, the call itself disappears.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the means, we will explain the case of switching to a lightweight model from a quality verification perspective.

screens.title: Case Commentary: Switching to a lightweight model made it faster, but the quality changed.
screens.lead: The instructor explains what to check when the delay is reduced after switching from a higher model to a lightweight model. Select the right arrow to follow the steps.

visual.alt: Side-by-side illustration of lag bars before and after model switching and an itemized quality comparison table.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: Switching from a large model to a lightweight model reduced the latency significantly. The development team wants to consider this a success. However, merely observing that latency has decreased does not confirm whether the switch was indeed appropriate.

steps.title: Step 1: Distinguish the causes of delay reduction
steps.body: We distinguish whether the delay reduction is due to the model being smaller, or because the lightweight model produces shorter responses. Since output is the largest contributor to latency, changes in output length alone can significantly affect latency. To properly assess the model's effectiveness, comparisons must be made under identical output length conditions.

steps.title: Step 2: Compare quality using the same evaluation set.
steps.body: We compare the quality of the two models using the same evaluation set. Instead of judging based on an overall average, we analyze on a per-item basis to identify where the quality deteriorates. It is essential not to judge solely based on the impression that one model has improved.

steps.title: Step 3: Missing items are supplemented with prompts.
steps.body: Defective items are improved by providing more detailed prompts, adding more examples, or fine-tuning. Smaller models can also perform well when properly used, matching the performance of larger models. After enhancement, the items are re-evaluated using the same evaluation set.

steps.title: Step 4: Still insufficient then
steps.body: Nevertheless, if capacity is insufficient, increase effort by leveraging more intelligence within the same model or routing only complex requests to the higher-tier model. It is not necessary to use the same model for all requests. Simple requests can be handled by lightweight models, while complex requests are managed by higher-tier models, thereby balancing latency and quality.

screens.outro: This time, we'll organize criteria for selecting effective means based on the situation.

screens.title: Selecting a potent means
screens.lead: Move the slider to try different sections with longer delays. For each section, the most effective method and the reason for its effectiveness will be displayed.

data.controlLabel: The interval with the greatest delay

stops.body: Output tokens are generated sequentially, making this the longest delay segment. Output pruning yields the greatest benefit. Request concise responses, simplify the grammatical structure of structured output, and cap the output with `max_tokens`. Reducing output tokens by 50% can reduce latency by nearly 50%.

Input trimming becomes important when inputs are very large, such as in documents or images. Unnecessary context is filtered out, and static content is moved to the front for caching. If the input is at a normal level, reducing input may only improve performance by 1% to 5%, so we should examine other areas instead.

Parallelization is effective when there are multiple independent requests. The total time is reduced to that of the single slowest request. For sequentially ordered stages, group them into a single prompt to reduce the number of round trips, or use speculative execution to mitigate delays.

Model grade is a major factor affecting speed, but it directly impacts quality as well, so it should be changed last, only after verification. First, adjust the effort, and when switching to a lightweight model, verify its quality using the same evaluation set. Smaller models can be enhanced with prompts and examples.

If it's difficult to reduce actual processing time, it makes users wait less. Streaming reduces waiting time to under one second, which is the most effective method. Displaying processing steps on screen and maintaining a loading state has a significant psychological effect, and both streaming and chunking actually advance the time when users finish reading.

screens.outro: With the criteria established, I'll conclude with the key points.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: Review the key points of this lesson on one screen. Read the paragraph below and proceed to the summary screen.

paragraphs: Delay can be divided into network, input processing, and output generation. The largest portion is typically output generation, so reducing output and sending independent requests in parallel is a typical approach.

Reducing the model tier significantly impacts performance, so we balance quality against speed using the same evaluation set. Adjusting trade-offs between intelligence, latency, and cost within a single model can be considered before considering model replacement.

Finally, delay can also be perceived as waiting by the user. Reducing perceptible waiting through streaming and progress indicators, and not relying on LLMs to handle tasks that can be systematically resolved, are ways to eliminate delay. Regardless of the method used, measurements should first be taken per segment, and after changes, both delay and quality should be re-verified together.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: After switching from a large model to a lightweight model, latency decreased. Before judging quality, what should we do first?
options: Distinguishes whether the latency reduction is due to the model or due to output length changes.
Delays have decreased, so immediately route all requests to the lightweight model.
Shortens the prompt without quality comparison
Reduce effort to further minimize delays, then compare.
checks.explain: First, distinguish the causes of delay, then compare the quality of the two models using the same evaluation set. For missing items, supplement them with prompts or examples or increase the effort.

wrong.1: Switching without verifying quality results in quality degradation.
wrong.2: You cannot verify effects or causes simply by reducing input without conducting a quality comparison.
wrong.3: Reducing delays without identifying the root cause or verifying quality is not in the correct order.

checks.incorrectFeedback: Unfortunately, this is not the correct answer.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Pair a significant means with its corresponding effect and context.
left: Want to trade latency for cost within the same model
checks.explain: Output is generated in sequence, so reducing it is effective; long inputs should be truncated or cached, independent requests should be sent in parallel, and effort is balanced within a single model.

glossary.def: Size, performance, and cost are different aspects of model layers. Smaller models are typically faster and cheaper.
The number of tokens generated by the model. The longer this number, the greater the delay.
This is a method where independent requests are sent simultaneously, reducing the overall waiting time to that of the slowest single request.
This is the time elapsed from when the request is sent until the first token appears. It affects perceived responsiveness during streaming.
This is a setting that balances intelligence, latency, and cost within a single model.

misconceptions.myth: Delay is caused by a slow model.
misconceptions.fact: Output length, requested structure, and input size also account for a significant portion. Particularly, output generation often constitutes the longest latency phase, so it must be measured per segment to identify the root cause.

misconceptions.myth: Small models always have low quality.
misconceptions.fact: Even small models can perform on par with larger models when enhanced with detailed prompts, shot examples, and fine-tuning. This should be verified and judged using the same evaluation dataset.

misconceptions.myth: Sending all requests in parallel speeds up the process.
misconceptions.fact: Parallelization is only applicable to requests that do not depend on each other. For steps that require the result of a previous step, ordering must be maintained, in which case request batching or speculative execution should be reviewed.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Delay is divided into network, input processing, and output generation.
Reducing output and parallelizing independent requests is a typical approach.
When reducing the model grade, quality is verified using the same evaluation dataset.
Effort adjustment is a means to consider before model replacement.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for your own reflection only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Which section of my app's response time likely accounts for the largest proportion?
